focus.text: English sorts nouns into two groups, and the group decides almost everything around them. Count nouns can be counted one by one, so they have a plural form and take *a* or a number: *one essay, three essays*. Uncountable nouns are treated as a mass, so they have no plural and no *a*: *advice, information, research, furniture, traffic*. The group also chooses the quantifier — *many essays* but *much advice* — and the verb: *the information is useful*, never *are*. Vietnamese does not make this split, so English nouns have to be learnt one by one.

summaryTable.caption: Count and uncountable nouns side by side

pretest.sentence: My teacher gave me some useful advice about the exam.
pretest.reason: *advice* is uncountable, so it takes *some* and no plural -s.

pretest.sentence: She sent me two informations about the scholarship.
pretest.reason: *information* is uncountable; count it with a unit noun: *two pieces of information*.

pretest.sentence: There are three students from Huế in my group.
pretest.reason: A number above one takes the plural form of a count noun.

pretest.sentence: We need to buy some new furnitures for the classroom.
pretest.reason: *furniture* has no plural form: *some new furniture*.

pretest.sentence: There are much problems with the old bus timetable.
pretest.reason: *problems* is a plural count noun, so it takes *many*.

pretest.sentence: I have a lot of homework this weekend.
pretest.reason: *a lot of* works with uncountable nouns such as *homework*.

pretest.sentence: My sister has read four book about climate change.
pretest.reason: A number above one needs the plural: *four books*.

pretest.sentence: The research on this topic is still very limited.
pretest.reason: *research* is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb.

pretest.reason: *bread* is uncountable; count it with a unit noun: *two loaves of bread*.

pretest.sentence: There is strong evidence that the new rule has reduced accidents.
pretest.reason: *evidence* is uncountable, so it takes *is* and no plural -s.

context.title: Advice from a cousin
context.paragraph: Before her first term in Đà Nẵng, Mai asked her older cousin for advice about living away from home. Her cousin sent three long messages full of practical information. She explained that flats near the university are expensive, so most students share a room and buy furniture second hand. She also warned Mai about the traffic on the coastal road, which is much worse in the rainy season. Mai made a list of everything she needed: two suitcases, a rice cooker, a few plates and a great deal of patience. She still had several questions, but she felt much less nervous after reading the messages.

sections.title: Forming plurals
notes: A count noun after a number, after *many, several, a few, both*, or after *one of*, is always plural: *three students*, *one of my friends*.
An uncountable noun never takes -s, however large the quantity is: *a lot of information*, not *informations*.

items.reason: A number above one takes the plural form.

items.stem: The teacher collected the ___ at the end of the lesson.
items.reason: *essay* is a count noun and adds -s in the plural.

items.stem: Two ___ from my class won prizes at the science fair.
She gave me a lot of useful ___ about the interview.
items.reason: *advice* is uncountable, so it never takes -s.

items.stem: We found three ___ of information about the scholarship.
items.reason: The unit noun takes the plural after a number: *three pieces of information*.

sections.title: Using quantifiers with each kind of noun

rules.text: Use *many*, *a few*, *several* and numbers with plural count nouns; use *much*, *a little* and *a great deal of* with uncountable nouns.

examples.text: The committee received **many applications** but **little funding**.
We still need **a few volunteers** and **a little more time**.

rules.text: *A lot of*, *plenty of*, *some* and *no* work with both kinds, which makes them useful when you are not sure.

examples.text: There is **a lot of traffic** on Cầu Giấy in the evening.
**A lot of students** cycle to school in Huế.

rules.text: *Much* is rare in positive statements. In writing, prefer *a lot of* or *a great deal of*, and keep *much* for negatives and questions.

examples.text: The project needs **a great deal of preparation**.
We do not have **much time** before the deadline.

tips: *A few* and *a little* mean 'some, and that is enough'. *Few* and *little* without *a* sound negative: *few students came* means almost nobody came.

items.stem: There are ___ tourists in Hội An in July.
items.reason: *tourists* is a plural count noun, so it takes *many*.

items.stem: She has made ___ progress since January.
Could you give me ___ about the entrance test?
Only ___ people came to the first meeting.
items.reason: *people* is a plural count noun, so it takes *a few*.

items.stem: We bought three ___ of bread for the trip.
items.reason: The unit noun takes the plural after a number: *three loaves of bread*.

sections.title: Forming quantity expressions for uncountable nouns

table.caption: Unit nouns that let you count an uncountable noun
rows: She gave me **two pieces of advice**.
a loaf of, a slice of
**Two loaves of bread** and **four slices of cake**
a bottle of, a litre of
a piece of, an item of
**One piece of news** about the flood

notes: *News*, *mathematics* and *physics* end in -s but are singular: *the news is good*, *mathematics is compulsory*.
The unit noun carries the plural, not the uncountable noun: *three pieces of advice*, never *three pieces of advices*.

items.sentence: There were much people at the station on Sunday evening.
items.reason: *people* is a plural count noun, so it takes *many*.

items.reason: *advice* is uncountable; count it with a unit noun.

items.sentence: The research on this subject are still at an early stage.
items.reason: *research* is uncountable, so the verb is singular.

items.reason: A number above one needs the plural form.

sections.title: Using nouns that work both ways, and academic uncountables

rules.text: Many nouns are uncountable as a substance or an idea, and countable when they mean a type of it or one item of it.

examples.text: Vietnam exports **coffee** to more than eighty countries.
The café sells **three coffees** from the Central Highlands.

rules.text: In academic writing, *research, evidence, advice, knowledge, equipment, feedback* and *work* stay uncountable and take a singular verb.

examples.text: The **evidence is** clear, although more **research is** needed.
Their **feedback was** detailed and very useful.

rules.text: To count those ideas, use a unit noun or a countable synonym: *a piece of research*, *two studies*, *three findings*, *a suggestion*.

examples.text: **Two studies** from Đà Nẵng reached the same conclusion.
Her supervisor gave her **three pieces of feedback** on the draft.

notes: *Work* is uncountable when it means effort (*a lot of work*) and countable when it means a piece of art or writing (*the works of a poet*).
tips: IELTS essays need *research*, *evidence* and *information* constantly. Learn them as singular: *research shows*, *the evidence suggests*. *Researches* and *evidences* are not used.

editing.text: Last month our club organised a workshop about studying abroad, and more than sixty student came. We invited two former members who are now at university in Australia. They gave us a lot of useful informations about visas, and they answered many question from the audience. One of them said that the biggest problem was not the money but the homeworks, because lecturers expect students to read a great deal before every class. She also gave three advices: start the application early, keep a copy of every document, and practise writing essays in English. Her advice were practical and easy to follow. There were much people at the end who wanted to talk to her, so we stayed an extra hour. My teacher say the workshop was the most useful event of the term. Next year we should to invite a student from Japan as well.

errors.reason: A number above one needs the plural form: *sixty students*.
*information* is uncountable and has no plural form.
*many* is followed by a plural count noun.
*homework* is uncountable, so it never takes -s.
*advice* is uncountable; count it with a unit noun.
*advice* is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb.
*people* is a plural count noun, so it takes *many*.
*My teacher* is he or she, so the verb takes -s.
A modal is followed by the base verb, with no *to*.

topics.prompt: A friend from another province is moving to your city for university. Write an email telling them what they will need to buy, what information they should collect before they arrive, and what advice you would give them about the first week.
checklist: *advice*, *information* and *furniture* appear with no -s and a singular verb.
Every count noun after a number or after *many* is plural.
*many* is used with count nouns, and *much* or *a lot of* with uncountable nouns.

topics.prompt: "Schools should set less homework and give students more free time." Give your view and support it with reasons.
checklist: At least two quantifiers are matched to the right noun type (*many hours*, *much time*).
Plural count nouns after numbers are written with -s.

topics.prompt: Describe a market, a supermarket or a small shop you know well. Say what is sold there, in what quantities, and who shops there.
checklist: At least three uncountable nouns are counted with a unit noun (*two kilos of rice*, *a bottle of fish sauce*).
At least three plural count nouns appear with numbers or with *several*.
No uncountable noun is written with -s.
